description: Scale a recipe for 20 or more people. Big factors, big pots, and the seasoning rule that keeps a crowd-sized batch from tasting flat or oversalted.

examples.result: The scaled pasta serves 24: 6 lb pasta, 12 cups sauce, 6 cups cheese, 12 cloves garlic.
steps: Multiply each amount by 6: 1 lb pasta becomes 6 lb, 2 cups sauce become 12 cups.
Cheese: 1 cup × 6 = 6 cups. Garlic: 2 cloves × 6 = 12 cloves.
examples.title: A pasta for 4, scaled to serve 24

examples.result: The scaled salad serves 30: 15 cups greens, 7 1/2 cups tomatoes, 5 cucumbers, 2 1/2 cups dressing.
steps: Multiply each amount by 5: 3 cups greens become 15 cups, 1 1/2 cups tomatoes become 7 1/2 cups.
examples.title: A salad for 6, scaled to serve 30

faqs.answer: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A recipe for 4 made for 24 has a factor of 6. Multiply every ingredient by 6, then season in stages rather than scaling the salt in full.
faqs.question: What is the scale factor for cooking for 24 people?

faqs.answer: Start with about three-quarters of the scaled amount, then taste and add more. Salt and strong spices are easy to overdo in a big batch, and a crowd-sized pot is the worst place to discover it.
faqs.question: How much salt goes in a recipe for a crowd?

faqs.answer: Yes, and for most dishes it is the better option. Two normal batches cook more evenly than one giant one, they are easier to handle, and if the first batch needs more seasoning, the second one gets it right. For soups and stews, one big pot works if you have it.
faqs.question: Should I cook in two batches instead of one big one?

faqs.answer: No. Cooking time follows thickness and pan size, not quantity. A bigger pot takes longer to come to a simmer, but the cooking time after that is about the same. Start early and check for doneness, not the clock.
faqs.question: Does cooking for a crowd take much longer?

faqs.answer: Weigh them. At a factor of 6, a cup of flour measured six times is slow and error prone. A scale is faster and exact. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, so a dozen eggs is about 600 g.
faqs.question: How do I measure big amounts accurately?

faqs.answer: Yes. Plan the storage before you cook: have containers ready, cool the extra food quickly, and freeze it in the sizes you will reheat. A crowd-sized cook is a gift to your future self, but only if the leftovers are stored properly.
faqs.question: What do I do with the leftovers from cooking for a crowd?

felicityNote: I have cooked for 24 in a home kitchen, and the secret is two batches and a written list. One giant pot is how dinner ends up late.

parts.meaning: The multiplier for every ingredient. From 4 to 24 servings, the factor is 6.
The number of servings you want to make. Here, 24.
The number of servings the recipe makes as written. Here, 4.
The amount of one ingredient after scaling.

formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. From 4 to 24 servings, the factor is 6.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A recipe for 4 made for 24 has a factor of 6.

howToSteps.name: Write the scaled list
howToSteps.text: Work down the ingredient list and multiply each amount by the factor. Write it down before you start, because big numbers are easy to lose track of.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the big amounts
howToSteps.text: At a factor of 6, measuring cups are slow and error prone. Weigh flour, sugar, and meat in grams or ounces instead.

howToSteps.name: Season in stages
howToSteps.text: Start salt and strong spices at about three-quarters of the scaled amount, then taste and add more. You can always add seasoning.

howToSteps.name: Cook in batches if needed
howToSteps.text: If the pot or pan is too full, split the batch. A crowded pan steams instead of browning, and a giant pot is hard to stir.

lede: Cooking for a crowd means a factor of 4, 6, or more. The maths is the same, but the pot, the seasoning, and the timing all need a second thought.

title: How to Scale a Recipe for a Crowd
tutorial: Cooking for a crowd is the same maths at a bigger factor. A recipe for 4 made for 24 has a factor of 6: every ingredient times 6. One cup becomes 6 cups. A teaspoon becomes 2 tablespoons. Two eggs become 12. The arithmetic is easy. What changes is everything around it: the size of the pot, the seasoning, the timing, and the sheer logistics of feeding two dozen people from a home kitchen.

The first decision is whether to cook one giant batch or two normal ones. For soups, stews, and braises, one big pot works if you have a pot big enough. For anything fried, roasted, or baked, two batches are almost always better. A crowded pan steams instead of browning, a giant tray of roast vegetables never crisps, and a tripled cake in one pan may never set in the middle. Two batches also give you a second chance: if the first one needs more salt, the second one gets it right.

Seasoning is the second decision, and it is the one that catches people out. Salt and strong spices do not scale the way flour does. Start with about three-quarters of the scaled amount, then taste and add more. A crowd-sized pot is the worst place to discover you have oversalted, because there is no fixing it and no second pot to dilute with. Taste at the end, not the beginning, because flavours concentrate as a big pot simmers.

Weighing is not optional at this size. Measuring 6 cups of flour one cup at a time is slow and error prone, and the error multiplies with the batch. A kitchen scale is faster and exact. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, so a dozen eggs is about 600 g, which is easier to check on a scale than to count twice. Write the scaled list down before you start, because big numbers are easy to lose track of halfway through.

A crowd-sized cook almost always means leftovers, and leftovers at this scale are a meal plan, not an afterthought. Plan the storage before you cook: have containers ready, cool the extra food quickly, and freeze it in the sizes you will actually reheat. Label everything with what it is and the date it went in. A freezer full of labelled containers is a week of dinners. A freezer full of mystery tubs is a chore you will put off.
